overview.title: 📖 Overview: From the Threshold to the Barber's Chair
overview.subtitle: Shabbat 9a–9b
overview.hebrewSource: לֹא יֵשֵׁב אָדָם לִפְנֵי הַסַּפָּר סָמוּךְ לַמִּנְחָה עַד שֶׁיִּתְפַּלֵּל
overview.label: The scene:
overview.text: Daf 9 closes out the sugya on domains by finishing the analysis of the threshold as an exempt domain — distinguishing an object that merely passes through its airspace from one that actually comes to rest there — and by explaining why a threshold's status flips between 'inside' and 'outside' depending on whether the door is open or locked. It also cites Rabbi Meir's decree against resting a burden atop a private-domain pillar, modeled on a parallel danger in the public domain. The daf then turns a corner entirely: a new mishna opens a fresh topic, listing activities — a haircut, the bathhouse, the tannery, a meal, a court case — that one may not begin close to the afternoon prayer, and the Gemara works out exactly which 'mincha' is meant and why.

slides.title: 🚪 Landing In vs. Passing Through
slides.subtitle: Why an exempt domain can break a transfer into two harmless halves

nodes.content: ❓ Rava ruled that carrying an object above the ten-handbreadth airspace of an exempt domain is still one continuous, liable act. Does the threshold, itself an exempt domain, work the same way?

columns.label: Merely passes through
columns.content: The object never rests in the exempt domain — the transfer stays ONE continuous act, and Rava's ruling makes him LIABLE

columns.label: Comes to rest there
columns.content: The object actually lands in the exempt domain — the transfer splits into TWO separate actions, neither of which is a Torah violation, so he is EXEMPT

nodes.content: ✅ This is exactly why a threshold can serve as a safe 'rest stop': an object set down there breaks the chain between private and public domain

callout.label: Distinction:
callout.text: It is not the exempt domain itself that grants safety — it is whether the object actually comes to rest inside it.

slides.title: 🏠 Why an Open Door Makes the Threshold 'Like Inside'
slides.subtitle: Two different accounts of Acherim's ruling
rows: An alleyway's threshold, half covered toward the inside and half uncovered
Open door: the roofing's edge counts as a lowered partition, sealing it as 'inside.' Locked door: no longer sealed, so it reverts to 'outside'
A house's threshold, covered by two beams (each under 4 handbreadths wide, less than 3 handbreadths apart), with a door between them
Open door: lavud joins the beams into one sealed roof-edge, treated as 'inside.' Locked door: the door separates them, so it reverts to 'outside'

callout.label: Common ground:
callout.text: Both answers preserve Rav Chama bar Gurya's rule that an opening needs its own post (לֶחִי) to be treated as sealed — they simply locate that 'post' differently.

slides.title: 🏛️ Two Domains That Are Legally One
slides.subtitle: Rabbi Meir's decree against a pillar standing inside a private domain

boxes.title: A Pillar Inside a Private Domain
items: Ten handbreadths high, four wide — by measurement, a full private domain of its own
Rabbi Meir: rabbinically forbidden to rest a burden atop it anyway

boxes.title: A Mound of the Same Size in the Public Domain
items: Lifting an object from the ground and placing it atop such a mound is a genuine Torah violation (carrying from public to private domain)
The Sages decreed against the pillar precisely so people would not confuse the two cases

callout.label: The principle:
callout.text: "Any place where you find two domains that are [legally] one" — even where Torah law would permit an action, the Sages sometimes forbid it by analogy to a genuinely forbidden parallel case.

slides.title: ✂️ Before the Barber, the Bathhouse, and the Judge
slides.subtitle: The new mishna: activities one may not begin close to mincha

callout.label: One exception cuts across all five:
callout.text: People interrupt any of these activities to recite Shema, but they do NOT interrupt them to recite the Amida prayer.

slides.title: 🕒 Which Mincha Does the Mishna Mean?
slides.subtitle: Reconciling the new mishna with Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi's stricter rule

lines.speaker: Gemara
lines.text: Which mincha does the mishna mean — mincha gedola (about half an hour after noon) or mincha ketana (about two and a half hours before sunset)?

lines.speaker: Gemara
lines.text: Not mincha gedola — there is still plenty of daylight left! It must mean mincha ketana.

lines.speaker: Gemara
lines.text: But that clashes with Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi: once the time for the afternoon prayer arrives, one may not taste anything before praying — implying he must stop even if he already began!

lines.speaker: Gemara
lines.text: Rather, the mishna DOES mean mincha gedola — but only for especially long versions of each activity: ben Elasa's elaborate haircut, a full bathing session, a large tannery's work, a big feast, the opening of a lengthy trial.

lines.speaker: Rav Acha bar Yaakov
lines.text: Actually, the mishna means even an ORDINARY haircut, still near mincha gedola — forbidden lest the scissors break, he faint in the bath, he spot a loss in the tannery and grow anxious, a small meal stretch on, or a verdict get overturned.

callout.label: Marking the start:
callout.text: The Gemara pins down exactly when each activity 'begins' — from placing the barber's wrap on one's knees, removing one's cloak, tying the tanner's apron, or (per Rav and Rabbi Chanina, reflecting Babylonian and Eretz Yisrael custom) washing hands or loosening one's belt for the meal.

summary.principle: An object that actually comes to rest in an exempt domain like a threshold breaks a transfer into two harmless halves, while mere passage through its airspace remains one liable act; and the new mishna's restriction on starting a haircut, bath, meal, or trial near mincha protects the primacy of prayer, whether read as mincha ketana generally or mincha gedola for lengthy versions of each activity.

flowSteps.content: 🚪 An object landing IN an exempt domain splits a transfer into two non-liable acts; merely passing through does not
🏠 A threshold flips between 'inside' and 'outside' depending on the door — via a roof's edge (Rav Yehuda) or lavud between beams (Rav Ashi)
🏛️ Rabbi Meir: a private-domain pillar is rabbinically off-limits, modeled on a genuinely forbidden public-domain mound

columns.content: ✂️ New mishna: no starting a haircut, bath, tannery visit, meal, or trial close to mincha
🕒 Resolved as mincha ketana generally, or mincha gedola for especially lengthy activities

flowSteps.content: 🎓 Key Principle: halakhic status turns on precise distinctions — resting versus passing, sealed versus open, ordinary versus lengthy — never on rough approximation

quiz.q: According to Rava's distinction, when does carrying an object through an exempt domain like a threshold escape Torah liability?
o: Whenever the object is food
Only when the object actually comes to rest in the exempt domain, splitting the transfer into two separate acts
Never — it is always liable
Only on Friday afternoon
quiz.e: If the object merely passes through the exempt domain's airspace without landing, the transfer remains one continuous act and he is liable; only an actual landing there breaks it into two non-liable halves.

quiz.q: According to Rav Yehuda citing Rav, what kind of threshold is Acherim's ruling (open door = 'inside') describing?
o: The threshold of the Temple
The threshold of an alleyway, half covered toward the inside and half uncovered
Any threshold whatsoever, without qualification
A threshold in the public domain only
quiz.e: Rav Yehuda explains that when the door is open, the covering's edge acts as a partition sealing the alleyway threshold as 'inside'; when locked, that sealing effect disappears.

quiz.q: Why does Rabbi Meir forbid resting a burden atop a ten-handbreadth, four-wide pillar standing INSIDE a private domain, even though the pillar is itself a private domain by measurement?
o: Because pillars are always forbidden on Shabbat
As a rabbinic decree, modeled on a mound of the same size in the public domain, where the same act would be a genuine Torah violation
Because the pillar lacks a roof
Because only priests may use pillars
quiz.e: The Sages forbade it lest people confuse this permitted case with the genuinely forbidden case of lifting an object onto a similarly sized mound in the public domain, which constitutes real carrying from public to private domain.

quiz.q: According to the mishna on 9b, which of these activities may one NOT begin close to the time of mincha, until he has prayed?
o: Only eating a meal
Sitting before the barber, entering the bathhouse or tannery, eating, and sitting in judgment
Only sitting in judgment
Only entering the bathhouse
quiz.e: The mishna lists all five: the barber, the bathhouse, the tannery, eating, and judgment — none may be begun close to mincha, though if already begun, one need not stop.

quiz.q: According to the mishna, what is the rule about interrupting one of these activities to pray once it has already begun?
o: One must always stop for both Shema and the Amida
One stops to recite Shema, but does not stop to recite the Amida prayer
One never stops for any prayer once an activity has begun
One stops only for the Amida, not for Shema
quiz.e: The mishna states the principle explicitly: people interrupt these activities for Shema, but not for the Amida prayer.
